title: Step-level policy rules must iterate step_entries(input), not input.jobs
answers: composite action steps skip policy checks
policy misses steps inside a composite action
why does a step rule not fire for steps in parallel groups
how do I write a new step-level check in policy.rego
body:
Symptom: a step-level policy violation (e.g. create-github-app-token without permissions, github-script without retries, ${{ }} in run) is not reported when the step lives in a composite action or a parallel group.
Root cause: .github/policy.rego step rules used `some job in input.jobs` + `job_steps(job)`, which only covers workflow job steps, so composite runs.steps and parallel children were never visited.
Fix pattern: iterate `some entry in step_entries(input)` then `step := entry.step`, and build messages from `entry.location` (positional, e.g. "job 'build', step #2") instead of job_id or step.name.
Constraints: step_entries(input) is the single traversal for workflow steps, parallel children, and composite-action steps; do not add a new per-job loop. Job-level rules (e.g. job if, push branches) are not step rules and still walk input.jobs directly.
applies: Any new or changed rule in .github/policy.rego that checks individual steps.
says: Workflow policy checks fail to catch security violations inside composite actions.
Pipeline compliance rules are skipping validation on steps running in parallel groups.
Enforce action and script policy checks across all composite action steps.
Why did the workflow linter miss policy infractions inside composite action definitions?
Ensure automated workflow security policies inspect parallel job steps.
search: Step-level policy rules in .github/policy.rego must iterate some entry in step_entries(input) and evaluate entry.step instead of traversing input.jobs and job_steps(job). Iterating step_entries(input) provides a single traversal that visits composite action steps (runs.steps) and parallel child steps, building diagnostic messages from entry.location. Rules must not introduce custom per-job loops, while job-level rules must continue walking input.jobs directly.
